title: Automate GitHub Models in Actions and the REST API
summary: Automate GitHub Models using GitHub Actions or REST API calls. Both methods require authentication with a token that includes the models permission.
body_markdown:
## Frequently asked questions


### Is GitHub Models free to automate?


Up to the documented rate limits, automating GitHub Models is free, which is why a scheduled workflow that fans out many calls will hit a 429 before it hits a bill.


**Treat the free tier as a prototyping allowance** . If a job needs more headroom, opt into paid usage rather than adding sleeps and hoping.


### Can I use my own API key with GitHub Models?


Not for the inference endpoint this article uses, which authenticates with GitHub credentials: a personal access token carrying the models permission, or the workflow token in Actions. A vendor key pasted into the Authorization header will be rejected.


If you want to call a provider directly with its own key, that's a different integration with its own billing and limits.


### Is GitHub Models suitable for production workloads?


It can be, but only on the paid path with retries built in. The free tier is designed for experimentation, and its limits are tuned for that.


Before you depend on it, add backoff on 429 and 5xx responses, set a timeout on every call, and decide what the job does when the model is unavailable.


A workflow that fails loudly and can be re-run is production-grade. One that silently skips the step isn't.


### Which models can I call from a workflow?


Whatever the GitHub Models catalog currently lists for your account, referenced by the model ID shown on its catalog page, usually publisher plus model name. Most often it goes wrong when a display name or a retired ID ends up in the request body.


Copy the ID from the catalog, or list the available models through the catalog endpoint, instead of typing it from memory. Availability and limits differ by model, so a call that works for one model can be throttled differently for another.


### Does GitHub Models train on my prompts?


According to GitHub's documentation, prompts and outputs aren't used to train the underlying models, and the model providers don't train on them either. Terms can differ by plan and by organization policy, so read the current data-handling statement before sending anything sensitive.


Whatever the policy says, keep secrets, customer records and credentials out of prompts. That's cheaper than auditing where they ended up.
